item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Hero veteran Virginia trooper rushes to help after car plows into women in crosswalk caught on video
item.description: Surveillance video shows a sedan plow into a court clerk and attorney in a downtown Richmond crosswalk as a Virginia state trooper rushed to help.
item.content:encoded:
A forgotten stack of court papers put a Virginia state trooper in the right place at the right time when a red sedan turned into a downtown Richmond crosswalk and sent two women tumbling off its hood.

Courthouse surveillance video shared by Virginia State Police shows the two women walking through a crosswalk on Clay Street when a red sedan makes a left turn and plows into them.

Both women roll off the hood and fall to the pavement as the car continues through the crosswalk.

ICE OFFICER HAILED AS HERO AFTER SAVING DRIVER INJURED IN MISSOURI CRASH

Trooper David Meehan, a 14-year veteran of the agency, saw the crash and rushed to keep traffic away from the injured women, state police said.

"Right place, right time!" Virginia State Police wrote on X. "We wish both a speedy recovery."

HEART-STOPPING VIDEO SHOWS OFFICERS USE UNLIKELY TOOL TO SAVE FAMILY TRAPPED IN FLOODWATERS

Meehan said in an interview shared by state police that he had left his summonses in his cruiser.

After court, he went back to get them and returned to the courthouse to drop them off.

SUSPECTED DRUNK DRIVER KILLS 2 PEDESTRIANS IN VIOLENT CHAIN-REACTION CRASH ON MANHATTAN'S UPPER WEST SIDE

"As I came out of the building, that’s when the crash occurred," Meehan said.

The women, identified in the video as a court clerk and an attorney, were seriously injured and are expected to make a full recovery, according to police.

DRAMATIC BODYCAM VIDEO CAPTURES NYPD OFFICER RESCUING WOMAN FROM TOP OF BROOKLYN BRIDGE AFTER EMOTIONAL PLEA

Meehan said Richmond police arrived and offered to handle the crash, but he stayed on the scene.

"As troopers, we are called to be selfless, engaged and aware," Meehan said. "And so witnessing something like that, it just made sense for me."

item.title: Al Gore buys hometown Tennessee newspaper, vows to preserve local outlet's 'independent voice'
item.description: Al Gore is buying the Carthage Courier, his hometown Tennessee newspaper, as the Lake family ends 50 years of ownership and all current staff are retained.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Al Gore is buying his hometown newspaper in Carthage, Tennessee.

The Carthage Courier announced Monday that the family of Hershel and Geraldine Lake will be handing the paper's ownership to Gore, and that an agreement and ownership transfer will be finalized in the coming weeks.

Carthage is roughly 60 miles east of Nashville.

20 YEARS LATER, AL GORE AND HIS DIRECTOR DEFEND THEIR CONTROVERSIAL CLIMATE MOVIE 'AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH'

"I’m so grateful to the Lake family for their decades of leadership in supporting independent news here in Smith County," Gore said in a statement. "Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community. When my hometown paper came up for sale, I saw an opportunity to help preserve the Courier as an independent voice for Carthage and Smith County."

"I look forward to supporting the Carthage Courier team, many of whom have served this community for decades, as they continue to provide vital information and serve this community for generations to come," he added.

AL GORE SAYS CLIMATE CHANGE SUPPORTERS ‘KEEP QUIET’ ABOUT THEIR BELIEFS FOR FEAR OF RETALIATION 

The Lake family put the Courier up for sale this fall after 50 years of operating the 113-year-old paper. Geraldine Lake died on Nov. 1 at 84.

The Courier also announced that its longtime publisher, Scott Winfree, will transition into a part-time role, citing health issues, and that newspaper advertising director Roger Wells will step in as the Courier's new publisher going forward.

The paper assured readers that publication will continue during the ownership transition and that all current staff will be retained.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

This isn't Gore's first foray into media. The former VP previously launched Current TV in 2005, which featured programs hosted by various media and political figures including Keith Olbermann, Joy Behar, Gavin Newsom, Jennifer Granholm and Eliot Spitzer.

The network was sold to Al Jazeera in 2013.

Before entering politics, Gore worked as a military journalist in the U.S. Army, serving during the Vietnam War, and later worked as an investigative reporter for The Tennessean.

item.title: Lions owner/chair emeritus Martha Firestone Ford dead at 101
item.description: The Detroit Lions matriarch took full control of the franchise in 2014 and backed the Inspire Change initiative, leaving a lasting mark on the city.
item.content:encoded:
Martha Firestone Ford, the owner and chair emeritus of the Detroit Lions, has died, the team announced. She was 101.

The team said Ford died surrounded by her family and loved ones.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Ford and her husband, William Clay Ford, received full control of the team in 1963 and she assumed full control of the Lions after he died in 2014. Ford transitioned to emeritus in 2020.

"In her most recent role as Owner/Chair Emeritus, Mrs. Ford supported her four children – Principal Owner/Chair Sheila Ford Hamp, Owner/Vice Chair Martha Ford Morse, Owner/Vice Chair William Clay Ford Jr., and Owner/Vice Chair Elizabeth Ford Kontulis – as they assumed leadership responsibilities within the family franchise," the team said in its obituary.

"Today the Ford family proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford, preserving the values, love, and passion that have shaped a family tradition spanning multiple generations."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Lions highlighted Ford’s charity work in the community. She backed the Detroit Lions Inspire Change initiative and held top positions in Merrill Palmer Skillman Institute, University Liggett School, Children's Home of Detroit and Edsel and Eleanor Ford House. She was also the founding member of the Henry Ford Maplegrove Center.

"It is with heavy hearts that we acknowledge the passing of Mattha Firestone Ford," the team sid in a statement. "Mrs. Ford inspired us all as a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team.

"She will always be remembered for her fierce loyalty to her family, her community and the city of Detroit."

Ford was a part of an exclusive club of pioneering businesswomen in the NFL as well.

She was among the group of NFL matriarchs that included the Chicago Bears’ Virginia Halas McCaskey, Pittsburgh Steelers’ Patricia Rooney and Kansas City Chiefs’ Norma Hunt.

"Her presence on our sideline, in our building, and in our community will be greatly missed. We wish the entire Ford and Firestone families peace in this time of mourning."

Ford is survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren and 17 great-grandchildren, according to the Lions.

item.title: Florida AG calls for doctor to lose medical license over 149 alleged illegal abortions
item.description: Florida's attorney general is pushing to revoke a North Miami Beach doctor's medical license, citing suspected violations of the Heartbeat Protection Act.
item.content:encoded:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is pushing to strip a North Miami Beach doctor of his medical license over at least 149 suspected illegal abortions, a number he says could rise to 180 as the investigation continues.

Uthmeier said in a video posted by his office on X that preliminary reports from state health officials indicate Dr. Sylvester Braithwaite allegedly performed the procedures between June 2024 and September 2026.

He said some may have been late-term abortions and called on the Florida Board of Medicine to revoke Braithwaite’s license.

DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

"A medical license is not a license to break the law," Uthmeier said.

Uthmeier cited Florida’s Heartbeat Protection Act and said none of the cases fell under the exceptions he outlined for medical emergencies or victims of rape, incest or human trafficking. He said each alleged violation amounts to a third-degree felony.

"My office is investigating this conduct, and we will follow the facts wherever they lead," Uthmeier said. "And we will prosecute doctors who ignore our laws."

Noah Brandt, executive vice president of the anti-abortion group Live Action, told Fox News Digital that Braithwaite should lose his medical license for good and face prosecution if investigators confirm the allegations.

"If these allegations are true, at least 149 innocent preborn children were killed in direct violation of Florida law, and each of those children deserves justice," Brandt said. "The killing of innocent human beings, including through abortion, should be illegal, and the fundamental human rights of every person, born and preborn, must be protected under the law."

‘YOU’RE FIRED’: NEARLY 40 PRO-LIFE GROUPS URGE TRUMP ADMIN TO CUT OFF PLANNED PARENTHOOD FUNDS

Brandt said Braithwaite should be "prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law" if the allegations are proven. 

He also praised Uthmeier for "his commitment to enforcing Florida’s pro-life laws and setting an example for attorneys general across the country."

Florida state Rep. Taylor Yarkosky backed Uthmeier in a reply on X, calling the alleged conduct "the Devil at work" and thanking the attorney general "for upholding the law in Florida, and mostly for protecting the lives of the unborn!"

Uthmeier did not say whether any charges had been filed or how far along the pregnancies were in the cases he described as potentially late-term.

Braithwaite is a board-certified obstetrician and gynecologist who serves as medical director of Women & Teens Healthcare in North Miami Beach, according to his professional biography. 

The Florida Department of Health lists his medical license as active and confirms his certification in obstetrics and gynecology.

Fox News Digital reached out to Braithwaite’s office for comment.

item.title: Piker backs idea to sell Trump on Medicare-for-all by calling it 'Trumpcare'
item.description: Hasan Piker backs Abdul El-Sayed's plan to pitch Medicare-for-all to Donald Trump as "Trumpcare," saying he has pushed the ego-appeal idea for years.
item.content:encoded:
Left-wing influencer Hasan Piker expressed support for Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s plan to get President Donald Trump to support Medicare-for-all by appealing to his ego and calling it "Trumpcare."

Speaking to liberal tech podcaster Kara Swisher on Monday, Piker lamented enduring the last two years of Trump’s term.

"He's [Trump's] so bad at everything," Piker said. "He's so incompetent, and all he cares about is enriching himself and his family. So, I don't know. I don't know where we go from here."

"We go to Trumpcare," Swisher quipped. "We go to Trumpcare for Medicare-for-all. That's what we're going to call it. That's the situation. Do you object to what El-Sayed said?"

HASAN PIKER DECLARES 'WOKE IS BACK,' FANTASIZES ABOUT PUTTING DONALD TRUMP IN PRISON

"No, I love it. I've been saying that for years," Piker replied. "Literally, I've been presenting this as a joke for, like, the last decade. I was like, ‘Look, you tell Donald Trump, what does Donald Trump love more than anything else?’ Undermining Obama's legacy. He loves his name. 

"He loves putting his name on stuff, and he loves undermining Obama's legacy. You pitch it to him as such. You say, ‘Look, Obamacare is done. This is better. Trumpcare is better. More comprehensive. Everyone will love you. You will be remembered as a legend."

"You're a genius," Swisher replied.

Earlier this month, El-Sayed posted a 16-second video urging the president to embrace Medicare-for-all and call it "Trumpcare."

UNEARTHED AUDIO EXPOSES STUNNING EL-SAYED ADMISSION ABOUT HIS HEALTHCARE PITCH

"Donald. Habibi. Midterms were rough. I get it," El-Sayed said in the video posted Nov. 17, addressing Trump with the Arabic term "habibi," commonly translated as "my dear" or "my beloved."

"Trumpcare-for-all. It's really popular. People really want healthcare. You can put your name all over it."

The video featured a mock "Trumpcare" card and an AI-generated image depicting Trump as Jesus Christ, which El-Sayed, a Muslim, referenced while urging the president to embrace socialized, taxpayer-funded healthcare.

"Donald, this is your chance to heal the sick (like in that one AI image. You know the one)," El-Sayed said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The White House responded at the time by blasting the pitch, warning that the Medicare-for-all proposal would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.

"The radical Democrats’ socialist proposal for a government takeover of healthcare should really be called ‘Medicare-for-none’ as it destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital.

Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during Trump's first term, spoke to Fox News Digital about the Piker's comments.

"Democrats just won historic victories, but they understand that they still have two years in which anything that’s going to get done has to go through Trump," he said. 

"Their simplistic assessment of Trump isn’t accurate and won’t work, but Republicans should read between the lines and forget stupid ideas like amnesty. Don’t give Democrats anything during these two years unless it’s a policy Republicans (and more importantly, Republican voters) actually want."

Republican consultant Mary Marslender reacted to Piker's commentary as well.

"Hasan Piker and his cronies are attempting to sell a government takeover of healthcare that would destroy the private innovation patients actually need," she wrote. 

"Trump has proven he only promotes policies that are good for our country, not policies that appeal to ego. He understands that Medicare-for-all would threaten access to breakthrough treatments, raise prices, limit choices, and deny Americans access to care."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and did not receive an immediate reply.

Fox News’ Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

item.title: Former NFL referee calls LSU 'deeply embarrassing' as school faces possible SEC expulsion vote
item.description: Lane Kiffin's first LSU season ends Saturday as the SEC schedules a Dec. 3 vote on terminating the school's membership, per an amended complaint.
item.content:encoded:
LSU’s first regular season under Lane Kiffin wraps up on Saturday when the Tigers face Arkansas in Fayetteville.

A football season that could end with no more than seven wins, amid controversy over the eligibility of former NFL players, has fallen well short of what LSU likely hoped for. But an even greater disappointment could be looming in Baton Rouge.

According to an amended complaint filed Monday in federal court in Alabama, the SEC has threatened to put LSU’s possible expulsion from the conference to a vote. Commissioner Greg Sankey has scheduled another special meeting for Dec. 3, "to consider the termination of LSU's membership in the SEC."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

If the vote takes place, LSU’s fate would rest with the conference’s chancellors and presidents.

Whether the school broke the conference's policies on professionalism on former NFL players has been called into question. However, LSU’s issues extend to its basketball program, where former NBA players have been added to the roster.

Former St. John’s player RJ Luis Jr. appeared in preseason games with the Boston Celtics last season. He played in one game for the Tigers, scoring 11 points ina a 79-67 Tigers win over Louisiana-Monroe last Wednesday. Shortly after the game, LSU President Wade Rousse said he told Tigers basketball coach Will Wade should not take the court in future games.

LSU POKED THE SEC BEAR, THEN FOLDED: RJ LUIS BENCHED AFTER CONFERENCE LEADERS DISCUSSED EXPULSION OR BOYCOTT

In an affidavit, Sankey said the conference will consider expelling LSU regardless of whether Luis remains sidelined.

NFL rules analyst Terry McAulay weighed in and offered a blunt criticism of his alma mater’s coaching decisions and alleged conference-rule violations. "LSU is my alma mater. I’ve had no relationship with them other than the normal affinity for one’s alma mater for decades," McAulay wrote in a post on X retweeting a statement from the SEC.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Their choice of head coaches in major sports and their recent behavior has been deeply embarrassing and they deserve whatever consequence may ensue."

The SEC defended its authority to govern its member schools and enforce its rules.

SEC ACCUSES LSU OF DEFYING ITS RULES AS WILL WADE’S BASKETBALL ROSTER ADDS FUEL TO A BURNING FIRE

"The lawsuit seeks to protect the Conference’s ability to govern itself and to enforce the rules and policies its member universities have voluntarily adopted," the statement from the conference read. "The Conference maintains its right to associate only with institutions that meet its established standards and expectations of membership and that demonstrate appropriate institutional control of their athletics programs. Monday’s filing advances the Conference’s obligation to defend its governance framework and the shared interests of its member universities."

The SEC was founded in 1932, with LSU being one of the conference's charter members.

The SEC first filed the lawsuit in September after LSU and Kiffin entertained adding former NFL players who had prevailed in similar eligibility court cases. The league held similar meetings that month, but LSU was not hit with any penalties at that time.

Under SEC bylaws, a school’s membership may be terminated involuntarily if at least two-thirds of the conference CEOs vote to do so at a meeting.

item.title: Tennessee jumps, Alabama drops, Indiana and UCLA tumble in new College Football Playoff top 25 poll
item.description: The Georgia Bulldogs hold No. 1 in the new College Football Playoff rankings, but chaos strikes as UCLA Bruins and Indiana Hoosiers suffer shocking losses.
item.content:encoded:
This week's iteration of the College Football Playoff selection committee Top 25 poll is out, and after a wild week in the Big Ten Conference, there are some major changes near the top of the rankings.

Well, not the very top, where the Georgia Bulldogs continue to sit at No. 1 after a dominant win over the questionably ranked South Carolina Gamecocks in Athens. The other top teams though? That's where the typical college football chaos reared its beautiful head yet again.

The Alabama Crimson Tide, a contentious pick in recent weeks at No. 3, saw their strength of schedule and resume take a step back as their conference wins either all lost or beat an FCS team. The UCLA Bruins, the most surprising team in the country and No. 4 heading into this week's poll, lost their first game of the season to the Michigan Wolverines.

ONCE AGAIN, THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF SELECTION COMMITTEE HAS AN OPPORTUNITY TO FIX THEIR MISTAKES

That loss came on the road and after the Bruins saw second-string quarterback Ty Dieffenbach go down with a lower body injury in overtime. Leading to Madden Iamaleava's disastrous mistake in the second overtime period. Which made the Bruins' status heading into a massive rivalry game against USC on Saturday one of the major storylines of the week.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Then there's the Indiana Hoosiers.

Head coach Curt Cignetti has been vocal in his criticism of the selection committee and their choices, for good reason, but the defending national champs finally got burned after weeks of playing with fire. The Hoosiers suffered a shocking defeat on the road against the Washington Huskies, their second of the season. And with a spot in the Big Ten Championship Game no longer a guarantee, their position in the rankings suddenly became a major talking point for their program and the conference.

BYU too, has struggled after their win over Notre Dame, escaping in triple overtime on the road against the Kansas Jayhawks. Would their seeming vulnerability in recent weeks cost them in the committee's eyes?

What about Tennessee? The Volunteers, despite their similar resume to Alabama and a head-to-head win, have sat behind the Tide in the rankings. Would the committee finally move them up? This week, they finally did.

Alabama fell three spots to No. 6, while Tennessee surged up four spots to No. 5. Wake Forest also finally got the boost they've been waiting for, leapfrogging UCLA and BYU to move to No. 8. Indiana fell a whopping six spots after losing to a now-ranked UW team on the road, and UCLA crashed to No. 9, meaning just one Big Ten team currently sits in the 12-team field. item.title: California prosecutors, victim advocates challenge Newsom's mass death sentence commutation
item.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom defended commuting 548 death sentences, but victims' advocates and a district attorney call the move morally offensive.
item.content:encoded:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom justified his blanket commutation of 548 death sentences to life without parole by arguing that reviewing cases individually would create "two classes of murder victims," a rationale victims' advocates and at least one district attorney called "morally offensive. "

Modoc County District Attorney Nina Salarno said Newsom's sweeping action denied the loved ones of murder victims any voice in the clemency process.

"I found it really offensive as a victim myself, and [for] my other victims," Salarno told Fox News Digital from Washington, D. C., where she and fellow advocates met with President Donald Trump this week. "There should be individual scrutiny. The individual victims should have a voice. And that's what he has avoided by doing a blanket commutation."

CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'

"The blanket commutation on a moral level as a victim I find very offensive, but I find the whole thing offensive to our entire rule of law," she added.

Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, a nonprofit that advocates for stricter laws against violent offenders, noted that California voters have repeatedly upheld the death penalty at the ballot box, including approving a 2016 measure aimed at speeding up executions.

"Here's a guy who throws rocks about kings and protests throughout the streets," Padilla said, referring to Newsom's past criticisms of Trump. "I will promise you, this is a move that is looked at and viewed as a king. He is trampling on the voters."

On Monday, Trump vowed to direct the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers and expedite federal executions as victims’ relatives spoke out at the Justice Department against Newsom's order.

SLAIN FIREFIGHTER'S MOTHER PLEADS WITH TRUMP TO INTERVENE AFTER NEWSOM STOPS KILLER'S DEATH SENTENCE

"Gavin Newsom and the radical left look at these heinous acts, and their sympathy is not for the children and their parents, but for the monsters who extinguished innocent young lives," Trump said. "He stood with the murderers and child slayers."

Justice for crime victims shouldn't be a partisan issue, Padilla said.

"Whether you're a Democrat or a Republican, you take politics out of this," he said. "The president of the United States stood up and sounded the alarm. And I hope the country hears it."

Newsom's office referred Fox News Digital to news release from Monday featuring victims and survivors who support his decision.

GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION

"As a member of the clergy, I believe that all life is sacred. I also believe in the possibility of redemption. Because of this, I oppose the death penalty," said Rabbi Suzanne Singer, the sister of Michele Reiner and sister-in-law of famed film director Rob Reiner, who were both stabbed to death in December 2025 inside their Los Angeles home. 

"As a civilized nation, it is barbaric that we still subject people to die at the hands of the state. I am so grateful to Governor Newsom for commuting the death sentences that have been imposed in our state. This is true proof of his moral character."

On Nov. 16, a coalition of roughly 30 county district attorneys, law enforcement groups, victims' rights advocates and grieving families filed a petition with the California Supreme Court seeking to halt Newsom's commutations.

MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

Salarno argued that the governor's move disrespects the jurors and judges who endured months-long capital trials. Even though California has not carried out an execution since 2006, Padilla noted that the death sentence itself provides essential legal validation and finality for grieving families, a loss he knows firsthand.

"The fact of the matter is the law is the law," Padilla said. "It's like changing the innings in a baseball game, changing from nine to seven retroactively, going back [and] going, 'I know you won that game, but we're going to make it seven innings and now you lost.'"

CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

The fight is also deeply personal for Salarno, whose older sister, Catina Rose Salarno, was murdered in 1979 on her first day at the University of the Pacific by her former high school boyfriend, Steven Burns. Following the tragedy, Salarno's mother, Harriet, founded Crime Victims United.

"Look, my sister's never coming back, and I understand that," Padilla added. "But I have to accept that she was murdered, like these families have to accept that their loved ones were. And we have to trust the justice system. And now it's been taken away from them. And that's where I think the real issue comes."

item.title: ICE nabs illegal immigrant days after he claims $1 million Massachusetts State Lottery prize
item.description: ICE sources say Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an El Salvador man with a 2014 deportation order, ran from officers in East Boston before his arrest.
item.content:encoded:
A man who smiled for a Massachusetts State Lottery photo with a $1 million check was arrested by federal immigration officers days later after a brief foot chase in East Boston.

Three ICE sources told Fox News that Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal immigrant from El Salvador, ran when officers moved in to arrest him early Tuesday but was quickly caught. 

Multiple officers’ body cameras captured the encounter, the sources said.

ICE ARRESTS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF RAPE, MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES AFTER RELEASE FROM MARYLAND JAIL

Velasquez-Morales had been wanted by ICE under a final deportation order issued in April 2014, the sources said. 

He crossed the U.S. border illegally near Roma, Texas, in 2013, according to the sources.

MASSACHUSETTS SUES TRUMP ADMIN TO STOP ICE'S COURTHOUSE ARRESTS: 'UNNECESSARY FEAR'

The Massachusetts State Lottery awarded Velasquez-Morales the $1 million prize Nov. 18, and posted a photo on Facebook three days later showing him holding the oversized check.

The lottery said he bought The Lottery's winning "$2,000,000 50X Cashword" $10 scratch ticket at a market in East Boston, the same neighborhood where ICE arrested him.

The Massachusetts State Lottery says anyone 18 or older can buy a ticket from a licensed retailer. The governor appoints two members of the five-member commission that oversees the lottery.

Fox News Digital reached out to Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey’s office and the lottery for comment.

item.title: Coast Guard searching for 2 children, 4 adults after plane crashes off Mississippi coast
item.description: A Cessna 210 Centurion with six people aboard went down roughly 2 miles northeast of Horn Island Tuesday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) rescue crews are conducting a search operation off the Mississippi Gulf Coast Tuesday after a plane carrying six people went down.

In a post on X, the U.S. Coast Guard Heartland said the Cessna 210 Centurion aircraft went down 2 miles northeast of Horn Island.

"[USCG] rescue crews are searching for a downed Cessna 210 Centurion aircraft with 6 people, 2 mi NE of Horn Island, Mississippi, after [USCG] watchstanders in Mobile received a report from [the Federal Aviation Administration], Tuesday," the U.S. Coast Guard Heartland said.

BODY WASHED ASHORE IN OREGON IDENTIFIED AS FORMER CITY COUNCILOR MISSING SINCE SEPTEMBER PLANE CRASH

A Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital the plane went down southwest of Pascagoula, Mississippi, at about 3:30 p.m. local time.

"The number of people on board is unknown at this time," the spokesperson said. "The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will investigate. The NTSB will lead the investigation and provide any updates."

FLORIDA LEARJET CRASH 911 CALLERS REPORT HEARING ‘BOMB’ AS PLANE CARRYING YOUNG FAMILY PLUNGES NEAR BUSY ROAD

The plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when it crashed, prompting an active search for four adults and two children between the ages of 8 and 12, according to local outlets WDSU and WLOX, citing the USCG.

The aircraft was traveling from New Orleans Lakefront Airport to Page Field in Fort Myers, Florida, when it dropped off FAA radar around 3:45 p.m., WLOX reported.

FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK

By 5:40 p.m., Coast Guard crews told WLOX they had located several pieces of wreckage, including the cabin, a life raft and three life jackets, though none of the passengers had been found.

A multi-agency response is underway in the area, according to the outlet.

The U.S. Coast Guard and NTSB could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

item.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asks federal judge to halt execution
item.description: Former U.S. Army Maj. Nidal Hasan filed a federal court motion Tuesday seeking to delay next week's scheduled execution at Fort Hood while he challenges his sentence.
item.content:encoded:
Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army officer slated to be executed next week for the 2009 murder of 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, has asked a federal judge to halt the execution while he mounts a legal challenge to his sentence.

The motion, filed in civilian court with the American Civil Liberties Union and the ACLU of Kansas acting as standby counsel, seeks a stay so Hasan can file a habeas corpus petition challenging the constitutionality of his death sentence.

Hasan remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE

"There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss. But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system," said Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, in a statement Tuesday.

"Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case," the statement continued. "We urge the court to stop the government from bypassing Mr. Hasan’s due process rights in its rush to carry out this execution."

Hasan is scheduled to be executed by an Army firing squad on Dec. 3 at the same Texas military installation where he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others. 

He was convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The execution would be the U.S. military's first in more than six decades.

SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire inside a medical processing building at Fort Hood —an attack he said was motivated by opposition to the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Now 56, Hasan uses a wheelchair after being left partially paralyzed when police officers shot him during his arrest nearly 17 years ago.

Plans surrounding the execution drew national controversy weeks ago after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially proposed livestreaming the firing squad. 

That proposal drew criticism across the political spectrum, with opponents warning a broadcast would fulfill Hasan's desire for martyrdom. President Donald Trump announced in October that the execution would not be livestreamed.

Meanwhile, the Army on Tuesday rejected appeals from three survivors of the 2009 shooting who had asked to witness the execution. Officials ruled that because the three were not physically wounded by gunfire, they were not considered direct victims under military execution regulations.

Retired Col. Kathy Platoni, who would have served as Hasan's supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal.

"I would desperately like to attend," Platoni said from her home in Ohio. "To look Hasan in the eye and say, ‘You didn’t get me.'"

item.title: Trump administration weighs targeting Iran's top regime leaders in bid to end war: report
item.description: Donald Trump's administration is reportedly weighing strikes on Iran's senior leaders, including Mojtaba Khamenei, as the war nears its ninth month.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration has renewed internal discussions about potentially targeting senior Iranian regime leaders in strikes that some officials believe could end the ongoing war, according to reports.

Citing a U. S. official and another source, NBC News reported Tuesday that some officials believe eliminating senior figures could pressure Tehran to end the conflict by showing that Washington can locate and strike the regime's leadership at any time.

Though the option has long been under consideration, it has "been under renewed discussion in recent weeks" as President Donald Trump deliberates over the next phase of the war, two sources told the outlet.

The deliberations come amid reports that Iran could be developing a radioactive "dirty bomb" and a report citing U. S. intelligence assessments of potential Iranian plots involving chemical weapons aimed at senior officials in Washington.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN ABOUT REPORTED PLOT AGAINST ADMIN OFFICIALS: 'WE TAKE IT VERY SERIOUSLY'

"We know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," Trump had told reporters at the White House Nov. 20.

Iran's surviving leadership includes Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, after the elder Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes of the war Feb. 28.

Other senior figures in Iran's military and national security apparatus include Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Commander Ahmad Vahidi, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander in chief reportedly appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026.

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

NBC News did not identify any of those officials as specific targets of the operations under discussion.

Administration officials opposed to the proposal have reportedly warned that targeting Iranian leaders could expose American officials to retaliatory attacks, stiffen the resolve of surviving regime figures and undermine future diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, now in its ninth month. 

The administration continues to weigh military options, enforce its naval blockade and assert control over the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

The debate comes months after U. S. and Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader and other senior military and intelligence officials, igniting a prolonged conflict centered on Tehran's nuclear program, ballistic missile capabilities and regional military activities.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who was reportedly injured in the strikes that killed his father, has not been seen publicly since assuming power, though he has warned Washington and Jerusalem against resuming major attacks on Iranian leadership.

MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS

"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," a statement attributed to Khamenei said.

The warning reportedly followed a meeting with senior Iranian military commanders, including Abdollahi, Hatami and Vahidi. On Oct. 31, Khamenei also directed Iran's armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any future threats.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing," a White House official told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

"The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Task Force Iron Gate will continue with full effect. 

"President Trump has many options at his disposal and will make the best possible decision to ensure Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon. "

item.title: Commanders coach Dan Quinn reacts to star wide receiver's explosive sideline outburst
item.description: Stefon Diggs was caught yelling "throw the f---ing ball" at Jayden Daniels during the Commanders' win, but coach Dan Quinn said he loves the fire.
item.content:encoded:
The line between providing motivation and being a bad teammate with a sideline outburst is a thin one.

Washington Commanders star wide receiver Stefon Diggs straddled that line during the team's thrilling 22-20 win over the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The four-time Pro Bowler appeared to be directing his ire toward Jayden Daniels on the sideline in the first half as the Commanders' offense was struggling.

Cameras caught Diggs yelling "throw the f---ing ball" after Daniels was sacked on a third down while Diggs appeared to be open. Commanders coach Dan Quinn had no issue with his wide receiver's outburst.

"I love his fire, I do," Quinn said, according to ESPN. "I love that. There's a lot of good that comes with it where it can sound like he's mad, but it's like some energy that comes behind it."

The Commanders are the fifth different team Diggs has played for in his 12-year career, and the sideline outbursts are something all of his prior teams are familiar with. Diggs' departure from the Buffalo Bills a few seasons ago centered on reported tensions with star quarterback Josh Allen from sideline outbursts.

Yet, for Quinn and his 4-5-1 Commanders, the energy that comes from Diggs is something he can deal with. For now.

The 56-year-old coach also said that "if something didn't feel right, I would step in and address it," according to NBC Sports.

Diggs had four catches for 45 yards in the Commanders' upset win. In 10 games this season, the 32-year-old has 40 catches for 431 yards and six touchdowns.

For Washington, the win was paramount in keeping their slim hopes of winning the NFC East alive. They are chasing the 6-3-1 New York Giants but do have the tiebreaker, should they end up with the same record.

item.title: Colorado Buffaloes coach Deion Sanders' latest arrogant comments raise serious concerns over ability to lead
item.description: Deion Sanders says he loses no sleep over Colorado's 4-7 season, claiming he is "winning life" as a $25.5 million buyout hangs after the UCF finale.
item.content:encoded:
Coach Prime wants everyone to know he sleeps just fine through Colorado's nose-dive.

Sitting at 4-7 ahead of Saturday's finale against UCF, Deion Sanders answered Tuesday's job-security questions with a shrug.

"Do you think that bothers me? Do you think that causes me to lose sleep or rest? Do you think that affects or infects my life?" Sanders told the media.

For a coach hired to build a powerhouse, it sounded a lot like waving the white flag. That kind of immaturity explains why his act has curdled during the back half of a spotty run in Boulder.

DEION SANDERS REPORTS THAT HE RECEIVES 'ABOUT FIVE' DEATH THREATS EVERY DAY AS COLORADO FOOTBALL COACH

He continued, "I've been on assignment for these kids, and if I'm not here longer, I'll move on to God's next assignment. So, that don't [sic] affect me like it may affect you or may affect some others. I'm in the third quarter of life. I may be losing games, but I'm winning life."

RANKING WHICH POWER 4 COLLEGE FOOTBALL HEAD COACHING JOB IS MOST LIKELY TO COME OPEN NEXT

Nobody gets paid millions of dollars in the Big 12 to preach from the podium while the program sinks. At this point, you have to ask whether Sanders was ever in this for the grind of coaching or just for the clout.

Still, if he truly does not lose sleep over losing, Colorado's brass may soon send him on to that next assignment.

item.title: Iran to execute 2 anti-regime protesters at dawn after 3 days in death row holding cells
item.description: Iran Human Rights urges UN intervention as two political prisoners await execution at Ghezel Hesar Prison in Iran's high-profile "Ekbatan case."
item.content:encoded:
Two Iranian anti-regime protesters face execution within hours after spending three days in pre-execution holding cells at Ghezel Hesar Prison, according to a human rights organization warning that the men were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and unfair trials.

Milad Armoun, 27, and Navid Najaran, 34, are scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO).

The men were transferred to solitary confinement on Nov. 21 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld their death sentences.

IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE

Both men were arrested during Iran's 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" uprising and are defendants in the high-profile "Ekbatan case," which stems from the killing of a member of Iran's Basij paramilitary force during nationwide anti-government demonstrations.

Exiled Iranian crown prince Reza Phahlavi said on X on Tuesday that the execution would take place at dawn.

IRANIAN REGIME CRITIC WARNS TRUMP DEAL COULD BE 'LIFELINE' FOR REGIME, CLAIMS PEOPLE ARE 'NERVOUS'

"Despite being acquitted of the murder charge, Milad Armon and Navid Najjaran have been sentenced to death by "hanging judge" Abolqasem Salavati.

"The execution orders for these two political prisoners have been sent to their lawyers, to be carried out at dawn on Wednesday, Azar 4."

"Milad and Navid were held in Ward 33 which houses those accused of murder before being transferred to solitary confinement in preparation for their executions today," a source told IHRNGO.

The men were sentenced to death in May by Branch 15 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, on charges of efsad-fil-arz , or "corruption on earth," a capital offense under Iranian law.

Salavati has faced longstanding criticism from human rights organizations over his handling of political cases and the harsh sentences imposed on government opponents.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, condemned the sentences and called for immediate international intervention.

"Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and grossly unfair trials. Their executions would be an irreversible injustice and another example of the Islamic Republic’s use of the death penalty as a tool of political repression.

IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS

"Strong international reactions may be the only way to save their lives. We urge the UN and all governments with diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic to intervene immediately to stop their executions," Amiry-Moghaddam said in a statement.

The Ekbatan case centers on the death of Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Aliverdi was injured during unrest in Tehran's Ekbatan neighborhood in 2022, and died two days later. Iranian authorities accused several protesters of involvement in his death.

Armoun was arrested in Tehran in November 2022, while Najaran was detained the following month in Ahvaz.

Iran Human Rights alleged that both men were tortured and subjected to ill-treatment to obtain self-incriminating confessions subsequently broadcast by Iranian state media.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Defense attorneys also accused judicial authorities of barring lawyers from hearings, withholding case documents and obstructing appeals.

Earlier death sentences tied to murder charges were overturned, and Najaran was acquitted of involvement in the killing in a separate proceeding. However, the Revolutionary Court subsequently imposed death sentences under Iran's national security laws.

The death sentences of two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, were overturned, and their cases referred for retrial, according to human rights organizations.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman detained by morality police over allegations that she improperly wore her hijab.

The demonstrations spread nationwide, becoming one of the most significant challenges to Iran's clerical leadership in decades.

item.title: FDA approves first new breast cancer hormone therapy in over two decades
item.description: Genentech says its oral drug Wilserdly reduced recurrence or death risk by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy in the Phase III lidERA breast cancer trial.
item.content:encoded:
A new early-stage breast cancer therapy has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the first time in more than two decades.

Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral hormone therapy from San Francisco-based drugmaker Genentech, received the approval after positive trial results in treating adults with early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.

This subtype is the most common form of the disease in which tumor growth is fueled by the hormone estrogen rather than excess levels of the HER2 protein.

NEW DRUG APPROACH OFFERS HOPE FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT AGGRESSIVE CANCERS

The Phase 3 lidERA study showed that the drug reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy, including generic pharmaceuticals like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, according to a Genentech press release.

Patients were also less likely to quit treatment because of side effects like joint pain and hot flashes compared to standard options, the researchers noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study found a reduction in cancer returning in distant parts of the body, like the bones, liver or lungs.

Aditya Bardia, M.D., global principal investigator of the lidERA breast cancer trial and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, noted that this finding is "particularly significant" because once breast cancer spreads to distant organs, it is "generally no longer curable."

The foundational hormone therapies used for early-stage breast cancer have remained "largely unchanged" since the 2000s, Bardia told Fox News Digital.

"These medicines have saved countless lives, but there has been room for improvement, both in terms of effectiveness and tolerability," he said.

"Now, for the first time in more than two decades, we have a new foundational hormone treatment that has been shown to be more effective than our existing standard therapies in early-stage breast cancer."

Because most breast cancers are caught early and fall into the hormone receptor-positive subtype, the new therapy has the potential to help a large number of patients, Bardia added.

Earlier this year, the FDA also approved Wilserdly combined with everolimus, an oral cancer medication, for the treatment of adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease had recurred during or after completing endocrine-based therapy.

This makes Wilserdly the "first and only" SERD (selective estrogen receptor degrader) that is FDA-approved to treat both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Levi Garraway, M.D., chief medical officer and head of global product development, commented in a statement that the FDA approval is due to the drug showing "superior efficacy" against other therapies that have long been the standard of care.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, plans to continue investing in "broad development" of Wilserdly, exploring its potential across disease stages and in new treatment combinations, according to Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham.

Bardia encouraged patients to speak with their oncologists about the new treatment option, particularly those whose recent diagnosis is "consistent with the regulatory label and approval of the drug. "

item.title: Kilmar Ábrego García to leave US voluntarily for Europe, avoiding forced deportation
item.description: Kilmar Ábrego García will voluntarily leave the United States for Spain to avoid deportation, sources say, capping a months-long legal battle with ICE.
item.content:encoded:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the illegal immigrant from El Salvador who became a rallying point for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies, will voluntarily leave the United States for Spain to avoid deportation, Fox News has learned.

Ábrego García is slated to depart for Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday night, sources told Fox News. He ultimately plans to make his way to Mexico, The New York Times reported, citing his attorneys.

The departure caps a months-long legal battle that began when he was initially deported to his home country and detained there.

TRUMP’S SPECIAL STRATEGY TO DEPORT ILLEGALS GIVES HIM ANOTHER TOOL FOR ENFORCEMENT

A federal judge in Maryland ordered Ábrego García to leave the U.S. by Tuesday, according to two sources familiar with the matter. That order remains under seal, and the exact terms of his release were not immediately clear.

The move comes after sustained efforts by the Trump administration to remove Ábrego García, who entered the U.S. illegally more than a decade ago. At one point during the legal proceedings, federal authorities sought to deport him to several African nations.

Ábrego García had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when immigration authorities detained him in March 2025. He was subsequently deported to El Salvador in error and held in the Central American nation's maximum-security CECOT prison despite a standing court order barring his removal there due to the risk of gang persecution.

Democrats rallied around him despite suspected ties to the MS-13 gang.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag. Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who visited Ábrego García while detained in El Salvador.

"While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation. I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution."

MIKE DAVIS: KILMAR ABREGO GARCIA, THE DEMOCRATS' PATRON SAINT OF HUMAN TRAFFICK

Federal officials eventually returned him to the U.S. to face human smuggling charges from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. He pleaded not guilty to the charges, which a judge later dismissed.

Throughout the legal fight, the administration maintained that Ábrego García was a gang member and pointed to a 2021 protective order his wife had filed against him over domestic violence allegations.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Ábrego García's attorney, the White House, the Department of Homeland Security and U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment.

item.title: Bill Maher declares late-night comedy is 'dead' after major political shift
item.description: HBO host Bill Maher agreed with Piers Morgan that late-night comedy was "dead," saying partisan hosts like Jimmy Kimmel won't play to half the country.
item.content:encoded:
HBO host and comedian Bill Maher told Piers Morgan Tuesday that late-night comedy was "dead" due to comedians focusing too much on one-sided political jokes.

Maher and Morgan discussed the state of late-night shows since Johnny Carson retired from "The Tonight Show" in 1992. Maher remarked that Carson likely retired at the right time before hosts and even entertainers became determined to force political messaging into their shows.

"Do you think that the likes of Jimmy Kimmel and the others, by being so obviously politically partisan, have they conspired to slightly kill late-night comedy for you?" Morgan asked Maher on "One on One with Piers Morgan."

JOHNNY CARSON'S FRIEND SAYS LATE-NIGHT KING WISELY AVOIDED PARTISANSHIP AS KIMMEL CONTROVERSY GROWS

"Well, it definitely seems dead," Maher said. "Yeah, so I don't think that helped. I know they don't like it when I say that, but it's true."

Maher remarked that he was always political on his programs but distanced himself from other late-night hosts since they had no interest in appealing to people outside their political circle.

"Now I'm like, 'Oh, I'm glad I'm not lumped in' because I'm not like them at all. I'm really not. And I'm not saying they're not talented or funny. They are. But, yeah, they absolutely have no interest in playing to half the country," Maher said.

Morgan pointed out that an overwhelming number of Kimmel's late-night political guests were not Republicans and that hosts like Kimmel rarely joke about Democrats.

LENO SAYS HE GETS 'BEAT UP' RHETORICALLY FOR REFUSING TO GO POLITICAL BUT REFUSES TO ALIENATE TRUMP AUDIENCES

"It's not like the left isn't doing a lot of stuff. And, of course, I've lost fans on the far left, and I don't miss them. You know what? Because if you don't understand what's wrong with your own side, you are watching the wrong show," Maher said.

Fox News Digital reached out to ABC and Kimmel's representative for comment.

Media Research Center President David Bozell agreed with Maher, citing his organization's history of documenting liberal bias on late-night shows.

"For years, MRC has documented just how predictable late-night television has become. The same people are always the punchline, and the same people are almost never the punchline. Somewhere along the way, the networks confused applause from a few hundred people in a studio with entertainment for millions of Americans at home," Bozell said.

BILL MAHER TELLS LIBERALS TO STOP 'PARTISAN SULKING' AND JOIN AMERICA 250 PARTY

Earlier this year, Maher suggested his friendship with Kimmel was on the rocks after he criticized Kimmel's wife, Molly McNearney, for cutting off family relationships based on whether they voted for President Donald Trump.

"This is the difference between the right and the left. It bugs me so much. My tribe is supposed to be the left, but these are the people who just can't talk to you unless you're exactly there," Maher said on his "Club Random" podcast.

Maher has also been a frequent critic of comedians and other entertainers interjecting politics into their performances to the point of alienating viewers.

"Don't tell me who I'm supposed to hate," Maher told Morgan.

item.title: Washington Commanders to host troubled WR Brandon Aiyuk for workout after clearing waivers from 49ers

He earned second-team All-Pro honors in 2023 before tearing his ACL and MCL in October 2024, sidelining him for more than two years.

When Aiyuk and Rosenhaus returned to San Francisco's business offices on Nov. 6 amid a $13 million bonus forfeiture dispute, both projected confidence about his return.

49ERS COACH GIVES BLUNT REACTION TO DISGRUNTLED BRANDON AIYUK'S RETURN TO TEAM: 'I COULD CARE LESS'

Arriving at the facility, Rosenhaus said, "We're here with all the right intentions." Aiyuk told reporters, "I'm feeling great, feeling healthy. It's been a long recovery process, a long rehab process, but I'm back to 100 percent and looking to get reinstated into the National Football League."

Exiting the sit-down, Rosenhaus offered only, "To be continued."

San Francisco ultimately waived him when his two-week roster exemption expired.

Still, signing Aiyuk carries serious baggage. Teams have questioned his character after he was arrested on charges of exhibition of speed by posting a video driving over 100 mph past Levi's Stadium.

Aiyuk also torched his exit in Santa Clara, calling head coach Kyle Shanahan "a toddler" and mocking Shanahan's July car crash on social media with posts reading, "You can't win the race if you crash out" and "stay in yo own lane."

Washington has unique familiarity to weigh that risk. General manager Adam Peters helped draft Aiyuk in 2020, and Daniels played with him at Arizona State before the two patched up their own social media rift last month.

If Aiyuk's knee checks out Wednesday, Washington could take a low-cost swing on a late-season run.

item.title: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary detailing spiritual crisis, encounters with the devil
item.description: Pope Francis' private diary reveals a two-year spiritual crisis from 2021, with the late pontiff writing he felt tempted by the devil and saw hell in 2018.
item.content:encoded:
Excerpts from the late Pope Francis' private diary published Tuesday reveal that the pontiff endured a two-year spiritual crisis beginning in 2021, writing that he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with the weight of wielding power over the Catholic Church.

The 160-page volume, "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," was compiled by Cardinal Victor Fernandez and spans entries from December 1992 through August 2024 — eight months before Francis died in April 2025 at age 88 — marking the first papal diary made public since the 1960s.

In a December 2022 entry, Francis described his crisis as "all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," adding that he resisted becoming a leader "who uses others like puppets."

MYSTERIOUS BLOOD-SOAKED RELIC LINKED TO HISTORY'S MOST BELOVED SAINT, ST. FRANCIS OF ASSISI, GOES ON DISPLAY

Across the entries, Francis wrote that he believed he had seen the devil three times — including during a Vatican meeting — and recalled a June 2018 vision of hell.

"Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote in the 2018 entry. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help."

Reacting Tuesday on "Varney & Co.," Fox News contributor and theologian Jonathan Morris said he was most struck not by the late pope's spiritual struggles, but by the Vatican's decision to publish them.

POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

"I think the most surprising part is that this was actually published, not so much that it happened, " Morris said. "Spiritual warfare is a very basic Christian doctrine, and even the last things — death, judgment, heaven, hell. And apparently he saw the gates of hell. Those are the core beliefs of the church across all sorts of denominations within Christianity."

Morris added that Francis' successor, Pope Leo XIV — whom Francis praised in the diary as "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man" — approved releasing the writings so they might help others facing similar trials.

Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: Unreal video shows Killer Whales delivering unusual gift to confused California paddleboarder
item.description: A paddle boarder in Monterey Bay, California got the thrill of a lifetime as two orcas surfaced beside him, one toting a torn-up sea lion carcass.
item.content:encoded:
Seeing a whale in the wild is something that most folks have on their bucket list.

It's not out of the ordinary for someone to book an Alaskan cruise or other whale-watching excursion while dropping thousands of dollars in the process.

If you're a little strapped for cash and can't make it all the way to Alaska, might I suggest paddleboarding with killer whales in Monterey Bay, California.

FIELD NOTES: KOE WETZEL BAGS A TEXAS GIANT, JACOB WHEELER GOES OFFSHORE & A WHALE VISITS NYC

That's exactly what one intrepid explorer experienced when he paddled into the open waters of California's Central Coast.

You can see the larger orca coming up from directly underneath the man's paddle board before being joined by a smaller counterpart.

MASSIVE 2,000-POUND SEA LION SHOCKS TOURISTS AT ICONIC US HOT SPOT: 'HE’S LIKE A VOLKSWAGEN!'

The smaller of the two orcas appears to be carrying the torn-up carcass of a sea lion.

Dinner and a show!

CALIFORNIA TEEN FACES PRISON AFTER VIRAL VIDEO SHOWS HIM SQUARING UP, REPEATEDLY KICKING SEA LION IN THE FACE

First and foremost, what a rush that must be seeing not one, but two killer whales up close and personal.

Some people go their entire lives without ever even seeing a whale off in the distance, and here's this guy getting a personal greeting from one of the ocean's most fearsome apex predators.

And speaking of predators, how about that absolute snack Shamu is carrying around?

Sea lions are pretty decent-sized marine mammals themselves, but this particular orca is tossing its lunch around like a football.

What's even crazier is that these two killer whales thought enough of their paddle boarding acquaintance to try and share their meal with him.

Much like a cat bringing a dead mouse to its owner, I think it's a really sweet gesture from the orcas to offer up a gift as a sign of good faith.

I know they're called "killer whales" for a reason, but these guys genuinely seemed like they were just stopping by to say "hello."

It's a story this California surfer will never forget.
