item.title: Major League Baseball players just called Rob Manfred's bluff with new proposal ahead of lockout | Ian Miller
item.description: Major League Baseball players agreed to share media revenues equally across 30 clubs, calling the owners' bluff on competitive balance as lockout looms.
item.content:encoded:
In just over one week, the 30 Major League Baseball owners will almost certainly lock players out of team facilities, pull down merchandise from their stores and generally act as though the players' fans pay to see don't exist.

There is no requirement that they do this, but it's become common practice for the league and ownership to enforce a "lockout" in hopes of pressuring the players to come to terms. This year's upcoming lockout, as has been widely reported, will revolve around the owners' desire to do a complete revamp of baseball's economic structure.

Baseball has no salary cap, unlike the NFL and NBA, which means players can earn whatever the free market decides they're worth. It's up to each ownership group to set a budget for themselves and determine what they're willing to spend. For some, it's worth paying exorbitant "luxury tax" penalties to sign higher-priced players.

MLB OWNERS ARE BACK WITH A NEW SALARY CAP PROPOSAL TO SHUT DOWN SPORT EVEN AFTER BREWERS WIN WORLD SERIES

For others, like Pittsburgh Pirates owner Bob Nutting, free agency is a once-a-decade experience, meant to sign a player here or there to a two-year contract in order to keep dozens of fans in their seats.

But one of the consequences of this free market system is that, unlike sports socialism, it limits franchise valuations. Because potential buyers of organizations in the NBA and NFL have certainty around what the top end of their outlays will be, they can justify paying higher ownership premiums. But in baseball, there's always the concern that fans might care about winning, which could require more spending. That's bad, you see, to care about a competitive sport, as it cuts into profits.

ONE OF MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL'S OWNERS JUST DESTROYED THE LEAGUE'S ENTIRE ARGUMENT FOR A LOCKOUT

Why these potential buyers don't just invest in other things, if they care so little about winning, is never brought up. But billionaires gonna billionaire, so here we sit in late November 2026, staring at the potential of a canceled 2027 season.

Another contention that owners make is that the league cannot achieve competitive balance without the creation of a salary cap. Teams like the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining baseball by signing players and winning, and teams like the New York Mets or Los Angeles Angels are also ruining baseball by signing players and losing. The Milwaukee Brewers, Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays don't exist, and players must limit their earning potential in order to make the Pirates, Rockies, and Marlins happy.

Their contention about "competitive balance" is factually wrong, first of all, as numerous analyses have demonstrated that payroll has the same added influence on winning as fielding a pitching staff that induces higher groundball rates. Which is to say, very little added influence.

There's also the fact that the Dodgers, for all their spending, are 3-14 since 2008 in the postseason, as far as winning the World Series goes, despite their exorbitant payroll. Or that the Padres, one of baseball's highest spenders over the past five years, have won one game in the NLCS for their troubles. Then there's the Mets, Giants and Angels. Or the Cubs who haven't even reached the NLCS since 2017. Boston has done little since 2018, and the Texas Rangers, from the massive Dallas metroplex, won in 2023 and haven't been back to the playoffs since. Houston won 81 games last year, and the Yankees haven't won the World Series in 17, going on 18, years.

All this is to say that there is no competitive balance problem to worry about. Owners have claimed there is anyway. And this week, the player's association called their bluff.

If, as the league claims, payroll differences are the cause of the nonexistent competitive balance problems, and that revenue disparities are the cause of those differences, the players just found the answer: share more revenue.

The owners recently claimed that sharing more revenue would allow the end of local blackouts, a nonsensical view that is totally unrelated to the actual cause of local blackouts. They also claimed that sharing more media income would close the gap between the rich and poor teams.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

So the players, in a new press release, said, essentially, "Great, we agree."

"Today, players reaffirmed their commitment to reaching a fair deal by agreeing to the owners’ proposal to share all MLB media revenues equally across the 30 clubs," their post said.

"The MLBPA also maintained its previous proposal to transfer hundreds of millions in additional non-media revenues from high-revenue teams to low-revenue teams, along with critical proposals meant to ensure all subsidies are used by front offices to improve the product on the field. Over the course of the next CBA, the players’ revenue-sharing proposals will increase assistance to low-revenue clubs by over $1 billion."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And there's the called bluff.

Owners don't actually care about competitive balanceor whether a small or big market team wins. They care about a salary cap because it will take a higher percentage of baseball revenue away from the players and redistribute it to them. It's the Zohran Mamdani model.

Particularly when considering that the league's proposal would exclude billions in ancillary baseball revenue, such as income from The Battery, a commercial development attached to Truist Park in Atlanta. The supposed "floor" would also include things like player benefits and expenses. Meaning that the supposed ~$171 million salary floor would be substantially lower, roughly $30 million, at least, lower in actual payroll.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Then there's the blackouts issue. A salary cap has nothing to do with local blackouts, but the Players Association's proposal ends that argument too. Redistribute more media revenue from big to small market teams, and end blackouts. Level the media playing field. Just keep a salary cap out of it.

If the owners were serious about competitive balance, which they of course are not, this would be a major step towards an agreement and a quick lockout. Or none at all. But because this has never been about competitive balance, we'll suddenly see the goalposts move. Quickly.

And again, salary cap or no, the cheap teams like the Pirates and Marlins will always spend the bare minimum. Competence is the biggest separator, which is why the Angels have been a disaster, despite having Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani on the same team, and why the Rockies' big deals have flopped, while the Brewers keep winning.

Spending less on players won't fix incompetence. But it will make owners more money, and that's, as always, what they really care about.

item.title: President of blue-collar coalition demanding higher pay, calls 'sub-minimum wage' a 'direct legacy of slavery'
item.description: One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman says the $2.13 tipped subminimum wage is a legacy of slavery as Democrats push a $25 living wage on Capitol Hill.
item.content:encoded:
One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman, who leads a coalition of lawmakers and blue-collar workers demanding a higher minimum wage, argued that paying a livable wage is an issue of racial and social justice.

"The subminimum wage for tipped workers is a direct legacy of slavery. It was created after emancipation," Jayaraman told Fox News Digital on Monday, arguing that the policy was designed "to allow restaurants to hire newly freed Black people for free, not pay them, and make them live on tips."

"Today, tipped workers are overwhelmingly women, single moms who work in restaurants like IHOP, Denny's and Chili's, struggle with three times the poverty rate, use food stamps at double the rate and suffer from the highest rates of sexual harassment because they have to put up with so much from customers to get tips.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

"So, what is social and racial justice?" she continued. "It is about allowing people to meet the cost of living. Everybody — White, Black, male, female — everybody deserves to earn enough to feed their families, and everybody deserves to earn that wage from their boss rather than having to put up with all kinds of crap from customers to get it from customers. Tips should be on top of a wage, as they are in several states, not instead of a wage."

One Fair Wage joined House Democrats and restaurant workers on Capitol Hill Nov. 18 to urge the incoming 120th Congress "to answer the affordability election with a $25 living wage and to make the Living Wage for All Act a Day One priority."

The current federal minimum wage has been set at $7.25 an hour since 2009, while the federal subminimum cash wage for tipped workers has remained frozen at $2.13 an hour since 1991. One Fair Wage is part of a national coalition of more than 100 organizations — including teachers' unions and progressive lawmakers — pushing for the $25 federal floor.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD

'CRAZY': MODERATES FEAR DEM LEADERSHIP PROMISED FAR-LEFT REPARATIONS AND ICE DEMANDS IN TURN OF VOTES

The Living Wage for All Act (H.R. 8555), introduced in April by lead sponsor Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., alongside co-leads, including Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., would phase in a $25 minimum wage over several years — reaching $25 for large employers by 2031 and smaller businesses by 2038 — while eliminating subminimum wage carve outs for tipped workers. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., introduced a companion bill in the Senate.

Mejia, a progressive backed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has championed far-left policies, including Medicare-for-all, a wealth tax and the abolition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The proposal, which would more than triple the current federal minimum wage, has raised concerns among critics and economists about potential job losses and the impact on small businesses in states with significantly lower living costs than major coastal cities.

"We should be rallying around $25 at minimum, and it should be cost-adjusted for inflation so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital on the day of the news conference.

FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE MANDATE WOULD DESTROY NEARLY 5M JOBS, HIT BOOMING SUN BELT HARDEST: STUDY

Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline. He said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."

Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat."

Jayaraman described the Nov. 3 midterm elections — in which Democrats captured majorities in both the House and the Senate — as a "blue-collar wave mandate" demanding a $25 federal minimum wage. She argued the push transcends racial and partisan lines and urged both Republicans and Democrats to listen to their constituents.

However, when the new Congress takes office in January, Democrats will remain well short of the two-thirds supermajority required in each chamber to override a presidential veto, setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing President Donald Trump to reject progressive legislation.
